title: Pediatric Podiatry
metaTitle: Pediatric Podiatrist in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor Kids
metaDescription: Looking for a pediatric podiatrist in Kirkland, WA? Run Doctor cares for kids' feet, from flat feet to heel pain and sports injuries. Call to book a visit.
summary: Kids' feet change fast as they grow. Our doctors help parents sort out normal growth from problems that need care, and we start with simple, gentle steps whenever we can.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Toddlers, school-age kids and active teens

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: As limping, tired legs, heel pain or clumsy walking

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A gentle exam and a talk with you and your child

overview: If you are looking for a pediatric podiatrist in Kirkland, WA, you are in the right place. Kids are not small adults. Their feet are still growing, and the bones, joints and growth plates change from year to year. That is why foot care for children needs a different eye. We want each child to feel at ease, so we keep visits calm, ask for your child's own words and never rush. Parents are part of every decision.

Many things you notice in your child's feet are normal for their age. Flat feet in toddlers and a wobbly walk are good examples. Still, some signs deserve a closer look, like pain, limping, toe walking that does not fade, or a child who stops wanting to play. Knowing what is normal can save you worry, and knowing what is not can save your child pain. Early answers often make care simpler.

At Run Doctor, Dr. Kate Cryderman and Dr. Lawrence Maurer see families from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and across the Eastside. Dr. Cryderman treats all ages and is a former college athlete. We explain what we see in plain words and start with conservative care first. Families can reach us at 425-899-3234. We welcome questions about growth, shoes, sports and anything else about your child's feet.
symptoms: Your child limps, or walks with a bounce or an odd pattern
Your child complains of foot, heel, arch or ankle pain
Your child often trips, falls or seems clumsier than other kids
Your child walks on tiptoes most of the time after the toddler years
Your child's feet turn in or out, or the arches look very flat
Your child avoids running or sports because their feet hurt
Shoes wear out in an uneven way or leave red marks on the feet

causes.title: Normal growth and development
causes.text: Feet change a lot from birth to the teen years. Flat arches, toeing in and a wide walk are common in young children and often settle on their own with time.

causes.title: Growth plate irritation
causes.text: Growth plates are softer areas near the ends of growing bones. Running and jumping can irritate them, most often at the heel in active kids, which may cause pain with sport.

causes.title: Foot shape and structure
causes.text: Some children are born with feet that are very flat, very high-arched or turned in a certain way. These shapes may be linked to pain, tiredness or changes in how they walk.

causes.title: Overuse from sport
causes.text: Kids who play on several teams or train all year can build up strain in the feet and ankles. Quick jumps in activity, hard fields and worn shoes can add to it.

causes.title: Muscle tightness or nerve and muscle conditions
causes.text: Tight calf muscles can affect how a child walks. Less often, a nerve or muscle condition plays a role, which is one reason we check how your child moves as a whole.

diagnosis: Your visit starts with a talk. We ask about your child's health, growth, sports, shoes and what you have noticed at home. Then we look at the feet, ankles, legs and hips, and check strength and flexibility. We watch your child stand, walk and sometimes run, so we can see how the feet work in motion. We may use video gait analysis for a closer look. If we need more detail, we may suggest an X-ray or other imaging. We explain what we find to you and to your child, and we tell you when we think a problem is likely normal growth.

treatments.title: Watchful waiting and guidance
treatments.text: When a finding is likely part of normal growth, we may simply track it. We tell you what to watch for and when to come back, so you are not left guessing.

treatments.title: Activity changes and rest
treatments.text: For pain tied to sport, we may suggest easing back for a short time, changing how much your child plays, or trying lower-impact activity while the area settles.

treatments.title: Shoe advice
treatments.text: The right shoe can make a big difference. We talk about fit, support and wear patterns, and help you choose shoes that suit your child's feet and sport.

treatments.title: Stretching and strengthening
treatments.text: Simple home exercises for the calf, foot and ankle may help with tightness or weakness. We show your child how to do them in a way that fits into busy days.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when needed
treatments.text: For some children, custom orthotics may support the feet and ease strain. We only suggest them when the exam shows they may help, and we check fit as your child grows.

treatments.title: Surgery only when it is the best option
treatments.text: Surgery is rarely the first step for children. We would only discuss it if conservative care has not helped or the problem needs it, and we would walk you through every choice.

whenToSeeUs: Your child limps for more than a few days, or limps with no clear cause
Foot or heel pain keeps your child from play, school or sport
Your child walks on tiptoes past about age 2 to 3, or the pattern is getting worse
There is swelling, redness, warmth or a lump on the foot or ankle after an injury
Your child's feet look very different from each other, or seem stiff or twisted
prevention: Choose shoes that fit well and check the fit often, since kids outgrow shoes fast
Build up sports time slowly, and plan rest days each week
Replace worn-out athletic shoes and use the right shoe for each sport
Let your child warm up and stretch before play
Take foot pain seriously, and let your child rest and tell you when something hurts

faqs.q: Do I need a pediatric podiatrist in Kirkland for my child's foot pain?
faqs.a: Not always, but it is wise to book a visit if pain lasts more than a few days, causes limping or stops play. A pediatric podiatrist in Kirkland, WA can check your child's feet, find the likely cause and tell you if it is just normal growth. Early advice often helps.

faqs.q: At what age should a child see a foot doctor?
faqs.a: There is no set age. A child can be seen at any age if you have a concern. Common reasons include limping, pain, toe walking that continues past toddler years, or feet that look very flat or twisted. Come when something worries you or your child's pediatrician suggests it.

faqs.q: Are flat feet in children a problem?
faqs.a: Usually not. Flexible flat feet are common in young children and are often a normal part of growth. The arch may develop over the years. We take a closer look if your child has pain, a stiff foot, tires easily or has changes in how they walk.

faqs.q: What happens at a child's first foot appointment?
faqs.a: The visit is calm and gentle. We ask about your child's health, activities and shoes, then examine the feet, legs and hips. We watch your child stand and walk. We explain what we see to you in plain words and talk through next steps together, if any are needed.

faqs.q: Will my child need surgery?
faqs.a: Most children do not. Foot problems in kids are usually managed with conservative care, such as shoe changes, stretching, activity changes or orthotics. Surgery is only an option if simple care has not helped or the problem needs it. We would explain every choice with you first.

title: Growing Heels (Sever's Disease)
metaTitle: Sever's Disease Heel Pain in Kids, Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Is your child's heel hurting during sports? Learn about Sever's disease heel pain in kids and how our Kirkland, WA doctors can help. Call Run Doctor to book.
h1: Sever's Disease Heel Pain in Kids: Care in Kirkland, WA
summary: Sever's disease is a common cause of heel pain in active, growing kids. It is an irritation of the growth plate in the heel, and it often eases with simple steps and time.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Active kids, often ages 8 to 14

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: At the back or bottom of the heel during sports

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Activity changes, stretching and a check of shoes

overview: Sever's disease heel pain in kids is one of the most common reasons active children get a sore heel. Its medical name is calcaneal apophysitis. The heel bone has a growth plate at the back, and in kids it is softer than the rest of the bone. Running and jumping can irritate it. Most parents first notice it as a child who starts to limp at practice or says their heel hurts after a game, then feels better the next day.

The name sounds scary, but it is not a true disease. It is an overuse problem tied to growth. It tends to show up in kids around ages 8 to 14, often during a growth spurt, when bones may grow faster than the muscles and tendons around them. Kids who play more than one sport, or who just began a new season, may be more likely to feel it. Boys and girls can both be affected.

Your child may limp after soccer, basketball, gymnastics or running. The pain often settles with rest. At our Kirkland office, we help families work out what is causing the heel pain and build a plan that keeps kids as active as is safe. We take your child's pain seriously, and we also know how much sport means to them, so our plans look for a safe way to keep playing.
symptoms: Pain at the back or bottom of the heel, often on one or both sides
Pain during or after running, jumping or sport
Limping after practice or at the end of the day
Tenderness when you squeeze the sides of the heel
Walking on tiptoes to avoid pressing on the heel
Heel stiffness or soreness first thing in the morning
Pain that eases with rest and returns when play starts again

causes.title: Growth spurts
causes.text: When bones grow fast, the calf muscle and Achilles tendon may become tight. That tightness can pull on the heel's growth plate and may irritate it.

causes.title: High-impact sports
causes.text: Soccer, basketball, running, gymnastics and similar sports mean many jumps and landings. Repeated impact on the heel adds strain to the growth plate.

causes.title: A sudden jump in activity
causes.text: A new season, a new sport or a tough camp can raise the load on the heel quickly. The growth plate may not have time to adapt.

causes.title: Shoes and playing surfaces
causes.text: Cleats, worn shoes or very flat shoes may give little cushion. Hard courts and fields can also raise the stress on a child's heel.

causes.title: Foot structure and how your child moves
causes.text: Very flat or very high arches and the way a child lands or runs may add stress to the heel. This is one reason we look at gait.

diagnosis: We start with your child's story: when the pain began, which sports they play, how much they train and what makes it better or worse. Then we examine the heel, calf, ankle and foot. We often gently press on the heel and test calf flexibility. We watch your child walk and may use video gait analysis. An X-ray is not always needed, but we may suggest one if we want to rule out other causes, such as a fracture. We do not diagnose from symptoms alone, so the exam matters.

treatments.title: Rest and activity changes
treatments.text: Easing back from the activity that hurts may help the heel settle. We talk about how much to cut back, so your child can stay as active as is safe.

treatments.title: Calf and heel stretching
treatments.text: Gentle calf stretches may reduce pull on the heel. We show your child how to do them and how often, and we keep the routine short so it gets done.

treatments.title: Heel cushions or heel lifts
treatments.text: A soft heel cup or small lift inside the shoe may reduce stress on the heel. We help pick the right option and check how your child feels in it.

treatments.title: Shoe review
treatments.text: We look at your child's everyday and sport shoes. Better fit, cushion and support may lower strain, and switching worn-out cleats can help too. We make sure the shoes are not too tight.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when needed
treatments.text: If foot structure appears to add to the problem, custom orthotics may support the heel and arch. We only recommend them if the exam points that way.

treatments.title: Further evaluation if pain lingers
treatments.text: If symptoms do not improve with care, we look again for other causes and talk through the next steps. Surgery is not a usual part of Sever's disease care.

whenToSeeUs: Heel pain lasts more than a couple of weeks, or keeps returning
Your child limps, or cannot play or take part in gym without pain
There was a hard fall or twist, followed by pain, swelling or bruising
Pain wakes your child at night or is present at rest
Only one heel hurts and it is getting worse, or the heel looks red or warm
prevention: Build up training slowly at the start of each season
Teach your child to stretch the calves before and after play
Use shoes that fit well and replace worn-out athletic shoes
Add rest days, and avoid playing the same sport all year without breaks
Let your child tell a coach and you early when the heels start to hurt

faqs.q: What is Sever's disease in kids?
faqs.a: Sever's disease is irritation of the growth plate at the back of the heel, also called calcaneal apophysitis. It is common in active kids, often around ages 8 to 14. It is not a true disease. It is an overuse problem linked to growth and sport, and it often improves with simple care.

faqs.q: How long does Sever's disease last?
faqs.a: It varies from child to child. Many kids feel better within a few weeks to a few months with care, and it usually fades once the growth plate matures. Pain can come back if activity ramps up too fast, so a plan for sport and stretching may help.

faqs.q: Can my child keep playing sports with Sever's disease?
faqs.a: Often yes, in a limited way, depending on pain. Some kids need to cut back or switch to lower-impact play for a while. We look at your child's sport, pain level and exam, then give clear advice on what is okay and what to avoid.

faqs.q: How do I know if heel pain is Sever's disease?
faqs.a: You cannot be sure at home. Pain at the back of the heel in an active child aged 8 to 14 fits the pattern, but other causes exist, including stress fractures. A podiatrist can examine the heel and decide what testing is needed.

faqs.q: Do kids with heel pain in Kirkland need an X-ray?
faqs.a: Not always. Sever's disease is often found by history and exam alone. We may suggest an X-ray if the pain is severe, follows an injury, is one-sided and worsening, or does not improve with care. The goal is to rule out other causes.

title: Flat Feet in Kids
metaTitle: Children's Flat Feet Treatment in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Worried about your child's flat feet? Learn when flat feet are normal and when to get checked. Our Kirkland, WA doctors offer children's flat feet treatment.
h1: Children's Flat Feet Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Flat feet are very common in young children, and most are flexible and not a problem. We help you tell normal arches from feet that may need care.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Babies, toddlers and young children

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: No pain at all, or tired feet and legs

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A foot exam and a look at how your child walks

overview: Many parents worry when they see their child's flat feet. The good news is that flat feet are common in young children, and most are flexible. A flexible flat foot shows an arch when your child sits or stands on tiptoes, and it flattens when they stand. That is often normal. Most of the time, a flexible flat foot needs no treatment. The goal of a visit is to be sure, and to give you peace of mind.

Babies are born with fat pads and loose joints that hide the arch. The arch often forms over the first years, though it may take longer for some kids. Many children with flat feet have no pain and run, jump and play just fine. Pain, stiffness and tired legs are the signs that matter most, more than how the arch looks in a photo or on the floor.

Some children do need a closer look. If your child has pain, tires fast, has a stiff foot or walks in a way that worries you, we can help. For children's flat feet treatment in Kirkland, our doctors check the whole picture and only advise care when it is likely to help. We also use video gait analysis when it helps, so we can see how your child's feet move while they walk and run.
symptoms: The arch is flat or low when your child stands
Feet or legs get tired or sore after play or a long day
Pain in the arch, heel or inner ankle
Ankles that roll inward when your child stands or walks
Shoes that wear down on the inner edge
Your child avoids running or keeping up with friends
A foot that feels stiff, or that stays flat even on tiptoes

causes.title: Normal development
causes.text: Young children often have flexible, loose joints and a soft pad under the arch. The arch usually develops with age, so flat feet at this stage are often normal.

causes.title: Family traits
causes.text: Foot shape often runs in families. If a parent or sibling has flat feet, your child may have them too, and it is often not a cause for concern.

causes.title: Loose joints or low muscle tone
causes.text: Some children have very flexible joints or lower muscle tone. This may let the arch drop more and may add to tiredness in the legs and feet.

causes.title: Tight calf muscles
causes.text: A tight calf can change how the foot moves and may increase arch stress. We often check calf flexibility as part of the exam.

causes.title: Rigid or less common conditions
causes.text: A stiff flat foot is different from a flexible one. It may be linked to bones that joined in an unusual way, and it needs a proper exam.

diagnosis: We begin by asking about pain, activity, family history and any past injuries. Then we look at your child's feet while they sit, stand and stand on tiptoes. We check whether the arch shows up when the foot is off the ground, test joint motion and calf flexibility, and watch your child walk and run. We may use video gait analysis. X-rays are not needed for most flexible flat feet, but may help if the foot is stiff, painful or looks unusual. We then explain what we find in plain words.

treatments.title: Reassurance and monitoring
treatments.text: For a flexible flat foot with no pain, the best plan may be to watch and recheck over time. We tell you which changes to look for so you know when to return.

treatments.title: Supportive shoes
treatments.text: Shoes with good fit and a firm heel may help comfort. We discuss what to look for in everyday and sport shoes, since kids outgrow them quickly.

treatments.title: Calf stretching and foot exercises
treatments.text: Simple stretches and play-based foot exercises may ease tightness and build strength. We keep them short and fun, so children will do them. We show you how to turn them into games.

treatments.title: Arch supports or custom orthotics
treatments.text: If your child has pain or tires easily, an arch support or custom orthotic may help the foot work better. We do not suggest them for every flat foot.

treatments.title: Activity guidance
treatments.text: If pain flares during sport, we may suggest changes in how much your child plays for a while, with a plan to return to full play step by step.

treatments.title: Surgery only in select cases
treatments.text: Surgery is rarely needed. It may be an option for a painful, rigid flat foot that has not improved with conservative care. We would go over every option with you.

whenToSeeUs: Your child has foot, arch or ankle pain with a flat foot
The foot is stiff and the arch does not show when your child rises on tiptoes
Your child limps, trips a lot or cannot keep up in play
The flat foot is only on one side, or looks different from the other
You notice swelling, redness or a bump on the inner side of the foot
prevention: Choose shoes that fit well and check fit as your child grows
Let your child go barefoot at home on safe surfaces to build foot strength
Encourage play like climbing, hopping and walking on tiptoes
Keep sport and activity changes gradual
Mention foot or leg tiredness early, so it does not get ignored

faqs.q: Are flat feet normal in children?
faqs.a: Yes, flat feet are common in young children, and most are flexible and normal for their age. Babies and toddlers often have no visible arch yet. The arch usually forms over the first years of life. It is worth a check if there is pain or stiffness.

faqs.q: Will my child outgrow flat feet?
faqs.a: Many children do develop an arch as they grow, but not all. Some people keep a low arch for life and feel fine. What matters most is whether the foot is flexible and pain-free. We can check your child and tell you what to expect.

faqs.q: Does my child need special shoes or orthotics for flat feet?
faqs.a: Not usually. A painless, flexible flat foot often needs only well-fitting shoes. Orthotics may help if your child has pain, tires easily or has other findings on exam. We recommend them only when we think they could help, not for every flat foot.

faqs.q: How do I check my child's flat feet at home?
faqs.a: Ask your child to stand on tiptoes while you look from behind. If an arch appears and the heel turns slightly in, the foot is probably flexible. If the foot stays flat and stiff, or hurts, book an exam. Home checks cannot replace a doctor's evaluation.

faqs.q: Where can I find children's flat feet treatment near Kirkland?
faqs.a: Our Kirkland office sees families from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and the wider Eastside. We look at your child's feet, explain whether the arch is likely normal and suggest care only when it is needed. Call 425-899-3234 to ask a question or book a visit.

title: Toe Walking in Children
metaTitle: Toe Walking in Children: Evaluation in Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Is your child walking on tiptoes? Learn about toe walking in children and when to get checked. Our Kirkland, WA foot doctors can help you find answers.
h1: Toe Walking in Children: Evaluation in Kirkland, WA
summary: Many toddlers walk on their toes for a while. If your child still does it after about age 2 to 3, an evaluation can help find the reason and guide next steps.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Toddlers learning to walk

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: As tiptoe steps, tight calves or a bouncy walk

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A full exam of the feet, legs and walking pattern

overview: Toe walking in children is common when kids first learn to walk. Many toddlers walk on their toes now and then, and most grow out of it. Your child may do it when excited, when walking barefoot or just for fun. It helps to note when it happens, such as in new shoes, on barefoot days or when excited, and to share a short phone video with us.

If your child still toe walks after about age 2 to 3, or does it most of the time, it is a good idea to get it checked. Persistent toe walking can have different causes. Some children simply have a habit. Others have tight calf muscles or a tight Achilles tendon. Starting early matters, because tight muscles can be easier to work with in younger children, and we like to find answers before habits set in.

Less often, it may be linked to a nerve, muscle or developmental condition, so a careful exam matters. We do not guess from a distance. At our Kirkland office, we look at how your child moves, explain what we find and work with your child's pediatrician when more input is needed. Our goal is to understand why your child toe walks, so the plan fits their needs and never relies on guesswork.
symptoms: Your child walks on their toes most of the time, not only now and then
Heels rarely touch the ground when walking or running
Calf muscles look tight, or the ankle feels stiff when moved
Your child trips or falls more than other children their age
Your child has trouble standing flat with heels down
Tiptoe walking started again after a time of normal walking
Walking looks different between the two legs

causes.title: Habit
causes.text: Some children get used to walking on their toes and keep doing it, even when their ankles move normally. It may be called idiopathic toe walking when no other cause is found.

causes.title: Tight calf muscles or Achilles tendon
causes.text: A short or tight calf can make it hard to get the heel down. Over time, toe walking may make the tightness worse.

causes.title: Sensory preferences
causes.text: Some children avoid the feel of the ground on their feet, or seek the pressure of tiptoe walking. This is one reason we ask about how your child reacts to textures and touch.

causes.title: Developmental or neurological conditions
causes.text: Toe walking can be linked to conditions that affect muscles, nerves or development. This is not common, but it is why a careful evaluation is worth doing.

causes.title: Family pattern
causes.text: Toe walking sometimes runs in families. If a parent or sibling walked on their toes as a child, it may help us understand your child's pattern.

diagnosis: We begin with a full history. We ask when your child started to walk, when toe walking began, whether it comes and goes, and about any family history. Then we examine the feet, ankles, legs and hips, check calf flexibility and ankle motion, and test strength and reflexes. We watch your child walk, run and stand, and may use video gait analysis. Sometimes we suggest more testing or a talk with your child's pediatrician or another specialist. We do not diagnose from one visit alone, and we explain each step to you.

treatments.title: Observation for young toddlers
treatments.text: If your child is very young and the exam is normal, we may suggest watching and rechecking. We tell you what to look for in the months ahead.

treatments.title: Stretching exercises
treatments.text: Gentle calf and ankle stretches may help if the muscles are tight. We show you how to make them part of play, such as animal walks and squats.

treatments.title: Shoe and insole changes
treatments.text: Certain shoes or inserts may help your child get the heel down. We choose these based on the exam and on how your child walks. We check the fit often.

treatments.title: Heel-down walking practice
treatments.text: Simple games and cues can help your child practice walking with heels down. Short, upbeat sessions often work better than long ones. We also review how your child feels about the ground.

treatments.title: Casting or bracing in some cases
treatments.text: If tightness is more fixed, a series of casts or a brace may be an option for some children. We would explain when and why before we suggest it. We would explain when and why before suggesting it to you.

treatments.title: Surgery as a last option
treatments.text: Surgery to lengthen a tight tendon is only considered when conservative care has not worked and the tightness limits function. We would discuss this with you carefully.

whenToSeeUs: Your child still walks on their toes most of the time after about age 2 to 3
Toe walking began after your child had already been walking flat-footed
Only one foot or leg is affected
Your child has stiff ankles, trips often, or seems weak or clumsy
Your child complains of leg or foot pain with walking
prevention: Encourage barefoot play on safe surfaces so your child feels the ground
Make heel-down games part of play, like crab walks and squats
Pick shoes that fit well and are flexible enough for natural steps
Gently remind your child to walk flat, without scolding or pressure
Keep regular checkups, and mention toe walking at well-child visits

faqs.q: Is toe walking normal in toddlers?
faqs.a: Yes, it is common in toddlers who are just learning to walk, and many grow out of it. Occasional toe walking is often fine. If your child still walks mostly on their toes after about age 2 to 3, an evaluation is wise to look for a cause.

faqs.q: When should I worry about toe walking in my child?
faqs.a: Seek an evaluation if toe walking continues past about age 2 to 3, happens most of the time, is on one side only or began after normal walking. Also act if your child seems stiff, weak or clumsy. These signs do not always mean a serious problem, but they need a check.

faqs.q: What causes toe walking in children?
faqs.a: There are several possible causes. Some children simply develop a habit. Others have tight calf muscles. Less often, it can be tied to nerve, muscle or developmental conditions. Because the causes differ, we do a full exam and do not guess, so your child gets the right plan.

faqs.q: Can toe walking in children be treated?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Treatment depends on the cause and your child's age. Options may include stretching, walking practice, shoe or insole changes, and sometimes casts or a brace. Many children improve with conservative care, though results vary. We explain each choice and what to expect.

faqs.q: Where can I get toe walking checked near Kirkland?
faqs.a: Our Kirkland office evaluates toe walking in children from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond, Bothell and nearby areas. We examine the feet, legs and walking pattern, and may coordinate with your child's pediatrician. Call 425-899-3234 to book a visit and talk through your concerns.

title: Youth Sports Injuries
metaTitle: Youth Sports Foot & Ankle Injuries in Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Learn about youth sports foot and ankle injuries, from sprains to growth plate pain. Our Kirkland, WA doctors help young athletes get safely back to play.
keywords: youth sports foot and ankle injuries
h1: Youth Sports Foot and Ankle Injuries in Kirkland, WA
summary: Young athletes can get foot and ankle injuries from sprains, overuse and growth-related pain. We help kids and teens heal and return to play with a clear, safe plan.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Kids and teens in running, jumping and cutting sports

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: As pain with play, swelling or a sore heel or ankle

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Rest from the painful activity and a proper exam

overview: Youth sports foot and ankle injuries are common, because kids run, jump, twist and land all day. Some injuries happen in one moment, like an ankle sprain. Others build up slowly from overuse, like shin pain or a sore heel. Kids often hide pain because they fear missing a game, so watch for limping, changes in how they run or a sudden wish to skip practice.

Growing bones add another layer. Growth plates are softer than adult bone, so a child's injury can differ from an adult's. Pain that seems minor may still need an exam. Playing through pain is not a good plan for a growing athlete. Many problems get better with simple care when they are caught early, and a short rest now may prevent a long break later.

At Run Doctor, both Dr. Maurer and Dr. Cryderman have a sports background, and Dr. Cryderman is a former college athlete. We see young athletes from Kirkland, Bellevue, Redmond, Woodinville and Bothell. We aim to find the cause, treat conservatively and help your child return to sport safely. We work with parents, coaches and trainers when it helps, so your child gets the same clear message everywhere.
symptoms: Pain that gets worse during sport and eases with rest
Swelling, bruising or tenderness around the ankle or foot
Heel pain after running or jumping
Pain in the shin, arch or the top of the foot
Limping, or trouble putting weight on the foot
An ankle that feels unstable or keeps rolling
Your child tells you they want to stop playing because of foot pain

causes.title: Ankle sprains
causes.text: A twist or roll can stretch or tear the ligaments around the ankle. Sprains are common in basketball, soccer, volleyball and trail running.

causes.title: Overuse and training load
causes.text: Too much play, too soon, may strain bones, tendons and growth plates. Year-round sport and playing on several teams can raise the risk.

causes.title: Growth plate irritation
causes.text: Growth plates in the heel and other areas can become irritated from repeated stress. This is a common reason for heel pain in active kids.

causes.title: Stress injuries to bone
causes.text: Repeated stress can lead to small cracks in bone, called stress fractures. They may feel like pain that builds with sport and does not fade with rest.

causes.title: Shoes, surfaces and foot mechanics
causes.text: Worn shoes, hard surfaces and the way your child's feet move can add strain. A gait and biomechanical exam may point to changes that help.

diagnosis: We ask how and when the injury started, which sport your child plays, how often they train and what makes the pain better or worse. Then we examine the foot, ankle and leg, checking swelling, tenderness, motion, strength and balance. We watch your child stand and walk, and may use video gait analysis to see how the feet move. If we suspect a fracture or other injury, we may suggest an X-ray or other imaging. After the exam, we explain the likely cause and the next steps.

treatments.title: Rest and activity changes
treatments.text: Time away from the painful activity gives tissue and growth plates time to settle. We help you plan how long to rest and what your child can do in the meantime.

treatments.title: Protective support
treatments.text: Depending on the injury, we may suggest a brace, tape, a walking boot or a supportive shoe. The goal is to protect the area while it heals.

treatments.title: Rehabilitation exercises
treatments.text: Strength, balance and flexibility work may help the ankle and foot heal and may lower the risk of another injury. We show your child exercises that fit their sport.

treatments.title: Shoe and gear review
treatments.text: We look at cleats, running shoes and court shoes. Worn or poorly fitting footwear may add to strain, and a better choice may help your child feel more comfortable.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics when needed
treatments.text: If foot mechanics seem to add to the problem, custom orthotics may help support the foot during sport. We recommend them only after an exam shows they may help.

treatments.title: Gradual return to play
treatments.text: We give a step-by-step plan to return to sport as pain settles. Surgery is only an option for certain injuries or when conservative care has not worked.

whenToSeeUs: Your child cannot put weight on the foot after an injury
There is clear swelling, bruising, deformity or a pop at the time of injury
Pain lasts more than a week or two, or keeps coming back with sport
Pain wakes your child at night or is present even at rest
Your child's ankle keeps rolling or feels unstable
prevention: Build up training slowly, and plan rest days and off-season breaks
Make sure your child warms up before practice and stretches after
Replace worn-out athletic shoes and use the right shoes for each sport
Encourage balance and strength work for the feet and ankles
Teach your child to speak up early when something hurts, and never to play through sharp pain

faqs.q: What are common foot and ankle injuries in young athletes?
faqs.a: Common injuries include ankle sprains, heel pain from growth plate irritation, shin pain and stress injuries to bone. Youth sports foot and ankle injuries often come from a sudden twist or from doing too much too soon. An exam can sort out the cause.

faqs.q: Should my child play through foot pain?
faqs.a: No. Pain is a signal to stop and get checked, especially in a growing child. Playing through pain can turn a small problem into a bigger one. Let your child rest from the painful activity and book an exam if pain lasts or limits play.

faqs.q: How do I know if my child's ankle injury is a sprain or a break?
faqs.a: You cannot tell for sure at home. Severe pain, swelling, bruising, a deformed look or trouble putting weight on the foot may mean more than a sprain. Because a child's growth plates can be injured too, it is wise to get an exam and possibly an X-ray.

faqs.q: How long before my child can return to sports?
faqs.a: It depends on the injury, your child's age and how well they heal. Some kids return in days, while others need weeks or longer. We give a step-by-step plan based on pain, strength and movement, so your child comes back safely rather than too soon.

faqs.q: Is there a doctor for youth sports injuries in Kirkland?
faqs.a: Yes. Our Kirkland office treats young athletes, and our doctors have sports backgrounds. We see kids and teens from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and across the Eastside for foot and ankle problems. Call 425-899-3234 to ask a question or book a visit.

title: In-Toeing and Out-Toeing (Pigeon-Toed)
metaTitle: Pigeon-Toed Kids: In-Toeing & Out-Toeing, Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Is your child pigeon-toed or walking with feet turned out? Learn about in-toeing and out-toeing in kids and when to see a podiatrist in Kirkland, WA.
h1: In-Toeing and Out-Toeing in Kids: Care in Kirkland, WA
summary: Many kids walk with their toes turned in (pigeon-toed) or turned out. Most cases are a normal part of growing and improve on their own, but a check can give you peace of mind.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Toddlers, young children and some teens

quickFacts.label: Often noticed
quickFacts.value: Tripping, W-sitting or feet that point inward or outward

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A gentle exam of the feet, legs and hips

overview: In-toeing, often called being pigeon-toed, means a child's feet point inward when they walk or run. Out-toeing means the feet point outward. Both are very common in children, and in most cases they are a normal stage of growth. Parents often notice it when a toddler starts to walk, or when an older child trips over their own feet.

The cause is usually found higher up in the leg, not in the foot itself. In-toeing may come from a twist in the shin bone, a twist in the thigh bone or the way a baby was positioned before birth. Out-toeing can come from the hips or from flat feet. Most children outgrow these patterns as their bones and muscles mature, but not all do.

At our Kirkland office, Dr. Kate Cryderman and Dr. Lawrence Maurer see kids from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and nearby. We check the whole leg, not just the foot, so we can tell what is normal and what needs a closer look. Most families leave with clear answers and a simple plan.
symptoms: Feet that point inward or outward when your child walks or runs
Frequent tripping or clumsy steps
Sitting in a W shape with the legs behind
Knees that point inward when standing
Shoes that wear out on one side
Complaints of tired legs after play
A limp or pain, which is not typical and should be checked

causes.title: Twist in the shin bone
causes.text: The shin bone can have a gentle twist that turns the foot inward. This often improves as a child grows.

causes.title: Twist in the thigh bone
causes.text: A twist in the thigh bone can turn the knees and feet inward. It is common between ages 3 and 8.

causes.title: Curved foot shape
causes.text: Some babies and toddlers have a foot that curves inward at the front. It often straightens with time.

causes.title: Hip position and flexibility
causes.text: Tight or very flexible hips can change how the legs turn. This can lead to in-toeing or out-toeing.

causes.title: Flat feet and sitting habits
causes.text: Flat feet can make the feet turn out. Long periods of W-sitting may also play a part in some kids.

diagnosis: We start by asking when you noticed the turning, whether it is getting better or worse and whether your child has pain. Then we look at how your child stands, walks and runs. We check the foot, shin, knee and hip, and measure how the legs rotate. Most children do not need an X-ray. We may suggest one or other tests if we see signs that point to a different problem. We do not guess from looks alone, so the exam matters.

treatments.title: Watch and wait
treatments.text: For many kids, the best plan is regular checks while they grow. Most in-toeing and out-toeing improve without treatment.

treatments.title: Sitting and play habits
treatments.text: We may suggest changing how your child sits, for example less W-sitting. Simple habits can help the legs rest in a better position.

treatments.title: Stretching and strengthening
treatments.text: Gentle exercises may help the hips and legs work well together. We show your child how to do them in a fun way.

treatments.title: Shoe and insert advice
treatments.text: Shoes or inserts may help if flat feet or poor support add to the problem. We choose them to fit your child's feet and activities.

treatments.title: Braces or surgery
treatments.text: These are rarely needed. We only talk about them if the turning is severe or causes real trouble, and we explain the pros and cons first.

whenToSeeUs: Your child limps or says their legs or feet hurt
The turning is getting worse, not better
Only one foot or leg turns in or out
Your child trips often or cannot keep up in play
The turning has not eased after age 8
You simply want a clear answer from a specialist
prevention: Encourage your child to sit cross-legged or on their heels instead of W-sitting
Choose shoes that fit well and have room for the toes
Keep up with regular checkups as your child grows
Offer plenty of active play, running and climbing
Bring your child's everyday shoes to the visit so we can check the wear

faqs.q: Will my child outgrow being pigeon-toed?
faqs.a: Most children do. In-toeing often improves by age 8 as the bones and muscles mature. A few kids keep a mild turn. Regular checks help us see how your child is doing.

faqs.q: Is W-sitting bad for my child?
faqs.a: W-sitting is common. It may keep the hips and legs in a position that supports in-toeing, so it is better to mix in other ways of sitting. Ask us if it worries you.

faqs.q: Do kids need braces or special shoes?
faqs.a: Usually not. Shoes and braces rarely change how the bones grow. We only suggest them when there is a clear reason.

faqs.q: Does in-toeing cause pain?
faqs.a: It usually does not. Pain, a limp or swelling is not typical and should be checked by a doctor.

faqs.q: What age should I bring my child in?
faqs.a: Any age. If you see a pattern that worries you, we are happy to take a look. Early checks give you answers and let us track changes over time.

title: Growing Pains and Leg Pain in Kids
metaTitle: Growing Pains in Kids' Legs & Feet, Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Does your child wake up with leg or foot pain at night? Learn about growing pains in kids and when to see a podiatrist in Kirkland, WA.
h1: Growing Pains in Kids: Care in Kirkland, WA
summary: Growing pains are common aches in the legs and feet of active kids, often at night. They are usually harmless, but pain that lasts or gets worse deserves a check.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Kids ages 3 to 12

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: In both legs, in the evening or at night

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: A gentle exam to rule out other causes

overview: Growing pains are aches or throbbing in the legs that many children feel, often in the calves, thighs or behind the knees. They tend to show up in the late afternoon or at night, then fade by morning. Many parents first notice it when a child complains after a busy day of running and play. The name can be misleading, because there is no proof that growth itself hurts. A tired, overworked muscle is a more likely cause.

True growing pains usually affect both legs, come and go and do not cause a limp. The child is back to normal play the next day. This pattern is common between ages 3 and 12, and it often settles by the teen years. Foot pain, pain in one spot or pain that lasts all day is different and needs a closer look.

At Run Doctor in Kirkland, we see many kids with leg and foot aches. Dr. Kate Cryderman and Dr. Lawrence Maurer take the time to find out what is behind the pain. Sometimes it is simple muscle fatigue. Other times it points to flat feet, tight muscles or a problem such as Sever's disease. We explain what we find in plain words, so you know what to do next.
symptoms: Aching or throbbing in both legs, often at night
Pain in the calves, thighs or behind the knees
Pain after a very active day
Pain that is gone by the morning
Kids who rub or hold their legs and want comfort
No limp and normal play the next day
Occasional foot or heel soreness after sports

causes.title: Tired muscles
causes.text: A long day of running, jumping and climbing can leave leg muscles sore. Kids often feel it once they slow down in the evening.

causes.title: Growth and tight muscles
causes.text: Bones may grow faster than muscles and tendons for a time. That can make muscles feel tight and sore.

causes.title: Flat feet or foot strain
causes.text: Kids with flat or very flexible feet may work their legs harder. This can add to evening aches.

causes.title: Sudden activity increases
causes.text: A new sport or a busy season can raise the load on young legs. Pain may follow a big weekend.

causes.title: Shoes that do not support well
causes.text: Worn shoes or shoes that do not fit may add strain. Checking the fit is an easy first step.

diagnosis: We start with your child's story: where the pain is, when it comes, how long it lasts and what helps. Then we examine the feet, ankles, legs and hips. We look at the arches, test muscle flexibility and watch your child walk and run. Growing pains are diagnosed by ruling out other problems, so we look for signs of injury, joint trouble or other causes. We may suggest an X-ray or other tests if the pain is not typical.

treatments.title: Comfort at home
treatments.text: Gentle massage, a warm bath or a heating pad on a low setting may soothe sore legs. Rest and extra cuddles help too.

treatments.title: Stretching
treatments.text: Short calf and thigh stretches may ease tight muscles. We show your child simple stretches they can do before bed.

treatments.title: Supportive shoes
treatments.text: Shoes with good fit and support may reduce strain. We help you choose shoes for daily wear and sport.

treatments.title: Inserts for flat feet
treatments.text: If flat feet add to the problem, an insert may help the foot work better. We only suggest one after an exam.

treatments.title: Pain relief guidance
treatments.text: Some families use over-the-counter pain medicine. Doses depend on your child's age and weight, so check the label and ask your child's doctor or pharmacist.

whenToSeeUs: Pain in only one leg or foot
Pain that lasts through the day or gets worse
A limp or trouble walking
Swelling, redness or warmth in a joint
Fever, rash or a child who seems unwell
Pain that wakes your child often over several weeks
Pain after a fall or injury
You want to be sure it is nothing more
prevention: Keep your child active, with a mix of activities
Replace worn-out shoes and check the fit often
Warm up and stretch before sports
Build up new sports slowly
Make sure your child gets enough sleep and fluids

faqs.q: Are growing pains real?
faqs.a: Kids do get leg aches that fit this pattern. The cause is not fully known, and growth itself may not be the reason. What matters is that true growing pains are mild and go away.

faqs.q: Why does it hurt at night?
faqs.a: Muscles can feel their tiredness when the busy day slows down. Kids notice aches more when they are still and quiet.

faqs.q: Can growing pains cause a limp?
faqs.a: No. A limp is not a typical sign of growing pains and should be checked.

faqs.q: Do flat feet cause growing pains?
faqs.a: They may add to leg fatigue in some children. We check the arches and may suggest shoes or inserts if needed.

faqs.q: When should I worry?
faqs.a: Pain in one leg, swelling, fever, a limp or pain that gets worse are signs to call a doctor. If you are unsure, we are happy to see your child.

title: Activity-Related Knee, Hip and Back Pain in Kids
metaTitle: Kids' Knee, Hip & Back Pain from Sports, Kirkland | Run Doctor
metaDescription: Does your young athlete have knee, hip or back pain after sports? Our Kirkland podiatrists look at feet and movement to find the cause.
h1: Activity-Related Knee, Hip and Back Pain in Kids: Care in Kirkland, WA
summary: Sore knees, hips or back after sports can start at the feet. We look at how your child's feet and legs move to find the cause and keep them active.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Active kids and teens who play sports

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: In the knee, hip or low back during or after play

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: An exam of the feet, legs, hips and the way your child moves

overview: Kids who run, jump and train hard can feel pain far from their feet. A sore knee, an achy hip or a tight lower back after soccer, basketball, track or dance is a common reason for a visit. Parents often notice it when a child slows down, avoids a favorite sport or complains after practice.

The body works as one chain. The feet meet the ground, and everything above them, including the ankles, knees, hips and back, reacts to how the feet move. Flat feet, high arches, tight calves or weak hip muscles can all change how force travels up the leg. Over time, that extra stress may show up as pain in a joint higher up. Growing bones can add to the problem, because muscles and tendons may be tight while the body grows.

At Run Doctor, we are a sports medicine practice. Dr. Kate Cryderman has a special interest in biomechanics, and Dr. Lawrence Maurer has years of experience with athletes. We examine your child from the ground up, including a gait and movement check. We look for the root cause of the pain, so your child can get back to the sport they love as safely as possible.
symptoms: Knee pain during or after running, jumping or squatting
Hip pain or a pinching feeling in the front or side of the hip
Low back pain that grows with sport or long sitting
Limping or favoring one leg
Pain that eases with rest and returns with play
Tight calves, thighs or hips
Feet that roll in or out during sports
Shoes that wear down unevenly

causes.title: Foot position and flat arches
causes.text: Feet that roll in a lot may twist the leg and add strain to the knee and hip. Some kids with flat feet have more leg fatigue.

causes.title: Tight or weak muscles
causes.text: Tight calves, hamstrings or hips, and weak core or hip muscles, may change how a child moves and strain a joint.

causes.title: Growth spurts
causes.text: When bones grow fast, muscles and tendons may feel tight. This can raise stress on the knee, hip and back.

causes.title: Too much, too soon
causes.text: Playing on several teams or jumping into a new season can overload young joints. Rest days matter.

causes.title: Shoes and playing surfaces
causes.text: Worn or poorly fitting shoes, and hard courts or fields, can add stress to the whole leg.

diagnosis: We begin by asking about your child's pain, sports, training load, shoes and any past injuries. Then we examine the feet, ankles, knees, hips and lower back. We test flexibility and strength, and watch your child stand, walk, run and squat. A video gait analysis may show how the feet and legs move during activity. We may suggest an X-ray or other tests, or ask another specialist to see your child, if the pain does not fit an overuse pattern. We never diagnose from one sign alone.

treatments.title: Activity changes and rest
treatments.text: We help you find the right balance. Your child may do less of the sport that hurts, while staying active in other ways.

treatments.title: Stretching and strengthening
treatments.text: Targeted exercises for the calves, hips and core may help the body share the load. We keep the plan short and doable.

treatments.title: Shoe review
treatments.text: We check your child's sport and everyday shoes. A better fit and the right support may lower strain.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: If the way the feet move adds stress up the leg, a custom orthotic may help. We only suggest one after an exam and gait check.

treatments.title: Return-to-sport plan
treatments.text: We help you build a gradual plan to return to play. We explain warning signs to watch for along the way.

whenToSeeUs: Pain that lasts more than a week or two
Pain that is getting worse
A limp or pain that wakes your child at night
Pain that stops your child from playing
Swelling, locking or giving way of the knee
Hip or back pain after a fall or hit
You want a sports and movement check for your child
prevention: Warm up and stretch before play
Rotate sports and take rest days
Replace worn-out athletic shoes
Increase training slowly
Build core, hip and leg strength with simple exercises
Tell a coach or parent early when something hurts

faqs.q: Can foot problems really cause knee, hip or back pain?
faqs.a: They may add to it. Feet are the base for the whole leg, and the way they move can change the load on the joints above. We look at the full picture.

faqs.q: Does my child need to stop sports?
faqs.a: Not always. Many kids can stay active with changes. We tell you what is safe and what to hold off on.

faqs.q: Will my child need an X-ray or MRI?
faqs.a: Not always. An exam often gives us a good answer. We suggest tests when the pain is not typical or does not improve.

faqs.q: Do you treat back and hip pain?
faqs.a: We look at how the feet and legs may add to it, and we can guide you on next steps. If a problem is outside our care, we help you find the right specialist.

faqs.q: What should we bring to the visit?
faqs.a: Bring your child's everyday shoes and sport shoes. Worn soles tell us a lot. Wear comfortable clothes that let us see the legs.
